children.value: This chapter asks how the events of the last trials carry over into what a participant reports and does next. The predictors are the outcomes of the attacks (bites, and among them bites without a net and bites despite a net in the attack slot), oddballs, transitions, the model-free prediction error and the surprise and uncertainty of three models: the latent-state model (Nexus), the change-point observer and the n-state model (

). The outcomes are the next in-task affect rating, the response to the next oddball, and the placement, gaze, cursor movement and pupil on the next trials. In the reverse direction, the affect rating is related to the placement on the trials after the rating screen. All effects are estimated within participants; the participants’ own lag slopes are then related to the general factor and to STICSA trait.

Run 23_11: 96 participants, 17,241 trials, 15,550 attacks (11,180 bites: 8,541 without and 2,639 despite a net in the attack slot), 1,507 oddballs, 768 transitions. Gaze for 87, pupil for 85 participants. Script:

entropy of the Nexus predictive distribution over the 32 slots before the outcome
1 − |2z − 1| of the state belief z before the outcome
uncertainty U of the believed direction before the outcome
Trials without an attack have no outcome; their outcome predictors are missing.

Lag 1, 2 and 3: the value on the trial one, two or three trials before the measured trial. Weighted: exponentially weighted mean over the preceding trials (half-life 3 trials, up to 10 trials, at least 3 with a value). For the ratings, the summaries cover the trials since the previous rating: the last trial with a value (lag 1), the plain mean (window) and the weighted mean ending at the rating trial.

Linear mixed models (maximum likelihood) with the predictor split into its within-participant part (participant-mean-centred, divided by its pooled within-participant SD) and the participant mean (z). Outcomes are divided by their pooled within-participant SD, so β is the change of the outcome in within-participant SD per within-participant SD of the predictor; tables also give β in the outcome’s unit. Every model contains trial number, condition and the previous value of the outcome; random intercept and random slope of the within-participant predictor per participant. If the random slope does not converge, the model is refitted with a random intercept; for the pupil outcomes, whose participant means are zero after the per-trial baseline, the random-intercept variance is zero and the models are OLS with participant-clustered standard errors.
the six ratings after trial 7 or 14 of each episode (0–100)
previous rating (the rating before trial 1 where it exists)

net entropy, slots with nets, split placement (nets at both state locations), log placement duration; gaze in the cue and placement windows; first cursor movement; pupil in the cue, placement and ISI windows
the outcome on the event trial (measured before its outcome) for lag L; its weighted mean with the same weights for the weighted summary
feedback and attack pupil on the oddball trial; shift of the next placement toward the oddball; net entropy and log placement duration on the trial after the oddball
the outcome at the previous oddball
mean over the three trials after the rating: net entropy, distance from the target, log placement duration, share of blocked attacks, direction changes of the first cursor movement
mean over the three trials up to the rating

Next-trial models also contain whether a rating screen preceded the trial. Pupil windows on trials after a rating or break screen are left out. The pupil models of the oddball family contain the outcome type of the oddball (blocked, bite despite a net, bite without a net), so that the feedback animation of the outcome is held constant. The rating screen follows trial 7 or 14 of an episode and never a transition trial, so the lag-1 transition models of the affect family are not estimable; the trial before an oddball is never an oddball or a transition, so the corresponding lag-1 models of the oddball family are not estimable.

Benjamini–Hochberg FDR. A family is the set of models that answer one question about one measure: one outcome (a rating, a next-trial measure, a response to the oddball), one lag summary (lag 1, 2, 3, window or weighted) and one class of predictors. The classes are the outcome events (bite, bite without a net, bite despite a net, oddball, transition; 5), the surprise and error signals (model-free |prediction error| and the surprise of the three models; 4), the uncertainty signals (4), and, for the rating → next trials models, the six ratings. The score tests use the same families, separately per score. All families are defined in

For the next-trial lag-1 models, each participant’s slope comes from an OLS fit of the same model (at least 30 trials) and is related to the score: slope (z) ~ score (z) + condition, HC3; β is the SD of the slope per SD of the score. The affect and reverse families have 8 or 9 ratings per participant (the nine in-task ratings, each with the previous rating as control; the first in-task rating has a previous rating only for the 23 participants whose results file contains the pre-task rating), the oddball family about 16 oddballs per participant; there the score enters the mixed model as a cross-level interaction (within-participant predictor × score), and β is the change of the within-participant slope (in the units of the main β) per SD of the score. With so few observations, the participant slopes from the random effects of these models (

) follow the participant’s mean rating (median |r| = .83, up to .98 for valence), so a regression of these slopes on the scores mainly reflects the relation of the mean rating to the scores; the cross-level interaction tests the dependence of the within-participant slope itself. Tested for the weighted summaries (affect, oddball) and for all reverse models. FDR within the families above, per score.
Ratings with a previous rating: 791 of 96 participants (8 or 9 per participant). Between two ratings lay a median of 20 trials with on average 12.8 bites (3.0 despite a net).
Rating ← events since the previous rating
24 of the 234 affect models reach q < .05 (32 p < .05); the table shows a selection, all are in

. Frustration rises and valence falls with the share of bites since the previous rating; the weighted summary, which gives the last trials the most weight, describes both better than the plain window mean and better than the last trial alone. Bites without a net and bites despite a net both raise frustration. Of the model signals, the surprise of the change-point observer relates most clearly to frustration, the surprise of Nexus (q = .005) and of the n-state model (β = .08, q = .042) less. Arousal rises after a higher predictive entropy and state uncertainty of Nexus (q = .016 and .045), and frustration after a higher uncertainty of the change-point observer (q = .038). Stress and fatigue show no effect with q < .05.

Most events change the placement, gaze and cursor movement on the next trial: q < .05 for 136 of 208 placement models, 172 of 312 gaze models, 73 of 208 cursor models and 35 of 156 pupil models (all lags and the weighted summary).

After a bite without a net participants use more slots on the next trial (β = .11 [.09, .13], +0.13 slots; net entropy .09 [.07, .11]); after a bite despite a net they use fewer (−.11 [−.12, −.09], −0.13 slots; net entropy −.10 [−.12, −.08]). Both effects remain at lag 2 and lag 3 (slots .06 and −.06) and are largest for the weighted summary (.10, −.12). The surprise of each model and the model-free error are followed by more slots and a higher net entropy (β .04 to .09 at lag 1, all q < .001), and by longer placements (Nexus surprise .05 [.04, .07]). After a transition, split placements with nets at both state locations are more frequent (lag 1 .09 [.05, .12], lag 2 .05 [.03, .07], lag 3 .02 [.00, .04]). Of the uncertainty signals, the state uncertainty of Nexus and the uncertainty of the n-state model are followed by more slots and longer placements (.03 to .05); the predictive entropy of Nexus by slightly shorter placements (−.02 [−.04, −.01]).

After an oddball, the gaze during placement rests less on the location of the current state (lag 1 −.13 [−.15, −.11], lag 2 −.08, lag 3 −.06, weighted −.15) and more on the other state’s location (.05 [.03, .08]) and on locations beyond the two states (.09 [.07, .12]). After a transition the share at the other state’s location rises on the next trial (.08 [.05, .11]) but not at lag 2 (−.01). Surprise of all three models has the same pattern as an oddball (current state −.11 to −.13; beyond the states .09 to .12) and raises the gaze entropy during placement (change-point observer .08 [.06, .10]); the gaze entropy is also higher after a bite without a net (.08) and lower after a bite despite a net (−.06). In the cue window the effects are smaller (|β| ≤ .06).

After a bite without a net, an oddball or a surprising outcome, the first cursor movement starts earlier (initiation time −.02 to −.03) and is more curved and changes direction more often (.03 to .05); the bite-without-net effect on direction changes is confined to lag 1 (lag 2 −.00, lag 3 .01). A higher predictive entropy of Nexus is followed by fewer direction changes (−.05 [−.07, −.03]), less curvature (−.04) and a lower cursor entropy in the cue window (−.06).

The placement pupil on the next trial is smaller after a bite (−.06 [−.08, −.04]), after an oddball (−.05) and after a surprising outcome (−.04 to −.05); the effect weakens at lag 2 (bite −.03, q = .044) and is absent at lag 3 (−.01). The ISI pupil is larger after a surprising outcome (Nexus .05 [.02, .07], q = .005; change-point observer .04 [.02, .07], q = .005). No outcome event changes the cue pupil with q < .05; the cue pupil is slightly larger two and three trials after a high model uncertainty (Nexus state uncertainty and n-state uncertainty, .02 to .03, q ≤ .031; weighted n-state uncertainty .03, q = .003).

children.value: Two of the 130 oddball models reach q < .05 (10 with p < .05). The placement after the oddball takes longer when the uncertainty of the change-point observer was high on the trial before (β = .09 [.04, .15], q = .002) and after larger model-free errors on the preceding trials (weighted .08 [.02, .13], q = .016). The events of the trials before an oddball do not change the feedback pupil (510 oddballs of 66 participants; largest: −.14 after high uncertainty of the n-state model, p = .015, q = .058) or the attack pupil (640 of 77) at the oddball, the shift of the next placement toward the oddball, or the net entropy after it (1,411 of 96).

Of the 221 next-trial lag-1 slopes, nine relate to the general factor with q < .05 and 13 to STICSA trait (family: one measure × predictor class, per score; all in

). STICSA trait adds gaze entropy at the cue after an oddball (.29, q = .034), fixations at the cue after the surprise of the change-point observer and of the n-state model (q = .020 and .007) and a smaller cue pupil after the surprise of Nexus (−.25, q = .038). Higher scorers spread their nets more after an oddball, look at more locations during the next cue and the next placement after a bite without a net, a large error or a surprising outcome, and have a smaller cue pupil on the next trial after a large prediction error; on average across participants these within-participant effects are small or absent (slots after an oddball .05, gaze entropy in the cue window after a bite without a net .02, cue pupil after a large error −.01), so the scores relate to how strongly a participant’s next trial depends on the event rather than to the average effect.

The within-participant effects of the outcome events and the surprise signals on the affect ratings do not depend on the scores. The uncertainty signals do: in higher scorers, anxiety rises less with the uncertainty of the change-point observer and of the n-state model (general factor −.09 and −.07, both q = .012; STICSA trait q = .034 and .012), frustration less with the uncertainty of the n-state model (−.11, q = .027) and arousal less with the state uncertainty of Nexus (−.09, q = .043; STICSA trait −.10, q = .023). These are 4 of 78 cross-level terms per score with q < .05 (family: rating × predictor class, per score). In the oddball family, the shift toward the oddball increases with the preceding uncertainty of the n-state model in higher scorers (general factor +.08, q = .035; 1 of 65). The rating → next trials effects do not depend on the scores (0 of 30).

Feedback pupil and the next trial.

For consecutive trials t and t+1 (t not after a rating or break screen), the next-trial measure was regressed on the feedback pupil of trial t. The model was y_{t+1} ~ pupil_w + surprise_w + |prediction error|_w + y_t + trial + bite type + condition + (1 + pupil_w | participant), a linear mixed model (ML).

pupil_w is the feedback pupil of trial t (500–2500 ms, pre-feedback baseline), centred within the participant and divided by its within-participant SD. The Nexus surprise and the model-free |prediction error| of trial t enter in the same form, so that pupil_w is the pupil response beyond the two signals it follows.
Outcomes (z-scored): slots with nets, net entropy, split placement, gaze entropy at the cue and gaze entropy during placement.
Score form: + q + q × pupil_w (cross-level), with the general factor or STICSA trait.
BH within each trial subset (all trials; bites without a net) over the five outcomes, separately for the within-participant effect and for each score’s cross-level term.

A larger feedback pupil goes with a higher gaze entropy during the next placement (all trials: +0.032 SD per SD [0.010, 0.055], p = .005, q = .025; bites without a net: +0.038, p = .010, q = .052; 85 participants).
Slots and net entropy tend in the same direction (+0.017, p = .051; +0.015, p = .085).
Split placements and gaze entropy at the cue do not (p ≥ .73).
None of these couplings depends on the general factor (cross-level terms |b| ≤ .018, all p ≥ .15, q ≥ .70) or on STICSA trait (all q ≥ .65).

After a bite through a correctly placed net, participants use fewer slots on the next trial (−0.11 within-participant SD per SD, q < .001; see above). The participant slopes of this narrowing are not related to the general factor (lag-1 participant slopes against the score, OLS with condition and HC3; BH within measure × predictor class, per score): slots −0.12 [−0.27, 0.03], p = .12, q = .31; net entropy −0.10, p = .13, q = .33; split placements −0.18, p = .072, q = .18. The estimates point to a slightly stronger narrowing in higher scorers.
Pre-cue baseline after a large error.

The pre-cue baseline of trial t+1 (not baseline-corrected) does not depend on the |prediction error| of trial t within participants (+0.006 SD per SD, p = .63). Its participant slopes are not related to the general factor (+0.12, p = .31) or STICSA trait (+0.18, p = .10). Model: covariates as above, random slope; participant slopes from OLS with at least 30 trials, related to the score with OLS, condition as covariate, HC3. In the same data, the cue pupil of t+1 (corrected to the 200 ms before the cue) has participant slopes on the error that are lower with the general factor (−0.28 [−0.47, −0.09], p = .004; STICSA trait −0.24, p = .020). The smaller cue response of higher scorers after large errors is therefore not a higher pre-cue level carried over from the error trial; it is a smaller dilation to the next cue.

The n-state surprise (without switches) relates less to the broadening slopes (ρ = .04 to .32), and its indirect effects include zero (

, participants whose pupils respond more strongly to surprising outcomes broaden their nets more on the next trial. With their pupil response controlled, the association of the general factor with this broadening falls by about one half to two thirds and is no longer significant.
, the gaze entropy at the next cue relates more weakly to the pupil response and keeps most of its association with the general factor.

The analysis is cross-sectional and uses the same participants for all three variables, so it shows that the pupil response and the net broadening share their score-related variance, not that one causes the other.

Frustration and valence at a rating screen follow the bites of the last trials, weighted toward the most recent ones; one SD more bites in the weighted window corresponds to 3.6 points more frustration and 1.5 points less valence. Both kinds of bites contribute. Among the model signals, outcome surprise relates to frustration; model uncertainty relates weakly to arousal and frustration.
The two kinds of bites have opposite consequences for the next placement.

A bite without a net is followed by wider placements, a broader gaze and more cursor direction changes; a bite despite a net, where the nets already were at the attack location, by more concentrated placements and a narrower gaze. Both persist over at least three trials.
Oddballs and surprising outcomes move the gaze away from the current state.

On the next placement the gaze rests less on the current state’s location and more on the other state and on locations beyond both, decaying over three trials; transitions shift the gaze to the other state’s location for one trial.
Little build-up toward the next oddball.

The events of the preceding trials do not change the pupil response to the next oddball or the shift toward it; only the placement after the oddball takes longer after high uncertainty of the change-point observer and after larger errors.
The rating itself is followed by slightly wider placements when frustration is high and valence low (both q = .037).

The scores relate to the strength of individual carry-over effects on the next trial — the net spread after an oddball, the gaze entropy and the number of fixations at the next cue and the gaze entropy during the next placement after a bite without a net, a large error or a surprising outcome, the cue pupil after a large error — and not to how affect follows the outcome events. Affect follows model uncertainty less in higher scorers (anxiety, frustration, arousal).
